claims.text: Enhanced oxidation resistance in multiprincipal-element high-temperature alloys is governed by preferential segregation of selected alloying elements at high temperature.
Slow diffusion of the selected elements contributes to maintained material integrity during high-temperature oxidation.
Cr and Al are characterized as refractory elements in the proposed alloy system.
Segregation of Cr or Al produces a continuous, adherent, and self-healing protective oxide scale in situ.
The initial alloy is well annealed and has a homogeneous, near-equiatomic microstructure containing Cr, Al, Ni, Co, and Fe.
The controlled comparison varies Cr or Al concentration while holding the other composition and processing parameters constant.
The proposed test range is 900–1100°C for 100–500 hours in an oxidizing atmosphere without significant applied mechanical stress.
Surface or grain-boundary segregation of the selected element facilitates formation of a continuous, dense, and adherent Cr2O3 or Al2O3 scale.
At high temperature, the selected alloying elements selectively oxidize at the surface.
The resulting oxide scale inhibits further oxygen ingress.
Inhibiting oxygen ingress mitigates oxidation-induced degradation and preserves microstructural integrity.
Increasing the selected element content will reduce oxidation-related weight gain relative to the equiatomic baseline.
Increasing the selected element content will reduce oxide-scale spallation relative to the baseline.
Increasing the selected element content will minimize microstructural degradation relative to the baseline.
The higher-content alloy will develop a more continuous and adherent protective oxide layer than the baseline.
The standard equiatomic baseline forms a less developed protective scale and consequently undergoes faster oxidation and greater degradation.
The proposed governing behavior is expected to hold between 900°C and 1100°C in oxidizing atmospheres.
Intrinsic oxide instability or catastrophic spallation may cause deviations at temperatures above the proposed range.
Severe applied mechanical stress may cause deviations from the proposed oxidation behavior.

Comparable oxide morphology, adherence, composition, weight gain, and microstructural degradation in the high-content and baseline alloys would falsify the proposed governing role of preferential segregation.
